chapters.title: Action and responsibility · Bhagavad Gita 2.47
chapters.body:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि॥२.४७॥
chapters.hindi:
तुम्हारा अधिकार अपने कर्म करने में है, उनके फल को अपने नियंत्रण में मानने में नहीं। केवल फल की इच्छा को कर्म का कारण मत बनाओ, और कर्म न करने की प्रवृत्ति से भी मत जुड़ो।

अभ्यास: पढ़ाई का समय और मेहनत तुम्हारे हाथ में हैं। परिणाम कई कारणों पर निर्भर करता है। आज के लिए एक ऐसा लक्ष्य लिखो जिसे तुम अपने प्रयास से पूरा कर सकते हो।
chapters.english:
Your responsibility lies in doing your work; its outcome is not entirely yours to command. Do not make the reward your only reason for acting, and do not become attached to avoiding action.

Practice: You can choose your study time and effort. Results depend on several factors. Write one goal for today that you can achieve through your own effort.

options: Act responsibly without attachment to results
questions.explanation: The verse links action with responsibility and warns against both attachment to outcomes and inaction.

questions.prompt: Which study goal focuses on action within your control?
questions.explanation: A planned period of revision is an action you can take; rank and others’ reactions are not fully under your control.

chapters.title: Input, processing and output
chapters.body:
A computer accepts input, processes it according to instructions, and produces output. Storage keeps information for later use.

When you type a calculation, the keyboard provides input, the processor performs the calculation, and the screen displays the output. Saving the result uses storage.

Hardware means physical parts. Software means the instructions and programs that run on the hardware. A browser is software; a keyboard is hardware.

questions.prompt: Which device is normally used for input?
questions.explanation: A keyboard sends the keys you press to the computer.
A browser is a program used to access websites.

courses.title: Linear Equations: Find the Unknown
courses.description: Understand equality, solve a one-variable equation and check your answer through a worked example. An original introductory sample in English.

chapters.title: Solving 2x + 3 = 11
chapters.body:
An equation states that two expressions have equal values. Think of the equals sign as a balanced scale. Whatever operation you apply to one side must also be applied to the other.

Solve 2x + 3 = 11. Subtract 3 from both sides: 2x = 8. Divide both sides by 2: x = 4.

Check your solution in the original equation: 2 × 4 + 3 = 11. Both sides match, so x = 4 is correct.

Try this: solve 3x + 2 = 14. Subtract 2, then divide by 3. You should obtain x = 4.

questions.explanation: Subtract 3 to obtain 2x = 8, then divide by 2.
Applying the same operation to both sides preserves equality.

chapters.title: Turn a word problem into an equation
chapters.body:
Three notebooks and a pen cost ₹65. The pen costs ₹5. If each notebook has the same price x, write 3x + 5 = 65.

Subtract 5: 3x = 60. Divide by 3: x = 20. Each notebook costs ₹20. Check: three notebooks cost ₹60; adding the ₹5 pen gives ₹65.

Practice: four identical pencils and a ₹6 eraser cost ₹30. Write 4x + 6 = 30, giving x = 6. Each pencil costs ₹6.

questions.prompt: Three notebooks plus a ₹5 pen cost ₹65. What is the notebook price?
questions.explanation: Remove ₹5 from ₹65 and divide the remaining ₹60 by three.

courses.title: Motion & Speed: Measure a Journey
courses.description: Learn to calculate average speed using distance and elapsed time, compare journeys and work with units. An original introductory sample in English.

chapters.title: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time
chapters.body:
Average speed describes how much distance is covered per unit of time. Divide total distance by total elapsed time. The time must be greater than zero.

A cyclist covers 120 metres in 20 seconds. Average speed = 120 ÷ 20 = 6 metres per second, written 6 m/s.

A walker travels 150 metres in 50 seconds. Average speed = 3 m/s. The cyclist has the higher average speed in these examples.

Average speed summarises the whole journey. It does not tell us that the cyclist travelled at exactly 6 m/s at every instant. Include any stops in the total elapsed time.

questions.prompt: What is the average speed over 120 m in 20 s?
questions.explanation: Divide 120 metres by 20 seconds to obtain 6 m/s.

questions.prompt: Which time belongs in an average-speed calculation?
questions.explanation: Use total elapsed time, including any stops during the journey.

chapters.title: Comparing speeds in different units
chapters.body:
To convert metres per second to kilometres per hour, multiply by 3.6. One hour contains 3600 seconds and one kilometre contains 1000 metres, so the conversion factor is 3600 ÷ 1000.

6 m/s = 6 × 3.6 = 21.6 km/h. To convert in the opposite direction, divide by 3.6. For example, 36 km/h = 10 m/s.

A 90 km journey taking 2 hours has average speed 45 km/h. Before comparing two speeds, convert them to the same units.
